screens.title: Data Transformation and Control Flow Activities
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to move beyond simple copies and design pipelines that think and adapt. Control flow activities give your pipeline decision-making power — they let you iterate over items, branch on conditions, and route work to different processing paths. Transformation activities let ADF call external compute, like stored procedures, Databricks notebooks, or Azure Functions, so heavy processing happens where it belongs. We'll show common patterns — lookup a set of files, iterate with ForEach, and run copies and transforms — and then cover retry policies and success or failure paths so the whole pipeline stays resilient. You will also see how parameters and variables make pipelines reusable across days, tables, and environments, and how expressions link activity output into later steps. A concrete use case we return to is processing daily sales files: use Lookup to get file names, ForEach to copy each file, then run a stored procedure to merge results. By the end you will recognize when to use control flow vs transformation activities and how to guard a pipeline with retries and failure handlers. Consider how your own ETL jobs could be made dynamic and more reliable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Data Transformation & Control Flow

Learn to route, iterate, and call external compute so pipelines are dynamic, reusable, and resilient.

Control Flow

Decisions, iteration, and routing: ForEach, If, Switch, Lookup.

Transformations

Invoke stored procedures, Databricks, or Functions for heavy processing.

Resilience

Use retries, failure paths, and explicit Fail activities to manage errors.

Parameters & Variables

Make pipelines reusable across dates, files, and environments.

Practical orientation

We will walk through a common pattern: Lookup files, iterate with ForEach, Copy each file, then run a stored procedure. Along the way, you will learn how to add retries and failure handlers so the pipeline recovers from transient errors.

Visual Concept
Static overview
Control Flow
Lookup → ForEach → Branching

Lookup produces a list that drives iterative work in ForEach, while If and Switch select alternate paths.

Transformations
Stored Proc · Databricks · Function

Choose the right compute: relational logic in stored procs, big data in Databricks, small custom code in Functions.

Resilience & Parameters
Retries, On Failure paths, Pipeline Parameters

Combine retry policies with explicit On Failure flows and parameters to build dependable, reusable pipelines.

Explore Key Topics
ForEach
Iterate over arrays returned by Lookup to process many files or tables.
Databricks
Run Spark notebooks for large-scale JSON or nested data transformations.
Retry & Failure
Use activity-level retry settings and On Failure paths to notify and stop cleanly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical pipeline design and reusable logic. First, you will learn to use control flow activities — ForEach, If Condition, and Switch — so pipelines can iterate and branch. That means you can process many files or route work to the correct ingestion path. Second, you'll integrate transformation activities such as Stored Procedure, Databricks Notebook, and Lookup to perform data processing where it is most efficient, whether inside a database or on a Spark cluster. Each objective includes why that skill matters: iteration reduces manual work, transformations centralize heavy compute, and branching keeps flows maintainable. You will also practice implementing error handling patterns and retry policies so transient failures don't cause service disruptions. Finally, you'll use parameters and variables to make pipelines flexible across schedules and environments, which reduces duplication and deployment friction. Each of these skills maps to a verified competency milestone so you can measure your progress and apply these patterns to real ingestion jobs.

screens.title: Control Flow Activities
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow activities define how and when work runs inside a pipeline. At a simple level, they are the glue that orders activities, evaluates conditions, and iterates over collections. Think of control flow as the program structure for pipeline orchestration: ForEach repeats a set of activities for each item in an array, If Condition chooses between two branches based on a boolean expression, and Switch selects among many branches based on a value. Lookup is often the source of truth for collections — it returns arrays that drive ForEach. These activities matter because real data integration rarely processes exactly one file or table; you often need to loop, branch, and make decisions based on metadata or runtime results. A common misconception is treating control flow like transformation: control flow does not change data; instead it controls which processing steps run. For example, you might use Lookup to fetch today's file list, then ForEach to copy each file, then a Switch to handle different source formats. Key takeaway: separate orchestration (control flow) from transformation so pipelines stay flexible and easier to debug. How would you test a branch that handles a rare source type?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Control flow activities manage order, branching, and iteration but do not themselves transform data.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Control Flow Activities
Core Concept

What control flow does

Control flow activities determine the pipeline execution order, branching, and iteration. They orchestrate work but do not perform heavy data transformation themselves.

Common activities
  • ForEach: iterate over an array.
  • If Condition: true/false branching.
  • Switch: select among multiple cases.
  • Lookup: retrieve arrays or single rows for decisions.
Common mistake
Using control flow to attempt data transformation. If you need to change formats or process records, call a transformation activity instead.
Illustration: orchestration cards
Lookup
Returns a list of file names or control table rows used to drive loops.
ForEach
Iterates over Lookup output and runs inner activities for each item.
If / Switch
Selects a path based on boolean checks or multiple case values.
Example scenario
Lookup returns two sales files; ForEach copies each one to staging; If Condition checks validation results before running a stored procedure.
Key Takeaway
Use control flow for ordering and decision-making, and pair it with transformation activities for data processing.

screens.title: ForEach Activity Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: ForEach is how you process many similar items with the same set of activities. The expected pattern is: first use a Lookup activity to return an array of items, then set the ForEach items property to that output so each entry becomes an iteration context. Inside the ForEach you can run Copy, Stored Procedure, Databricks, or any activity; each iteration sees its own current item accessible via item() expressions. A concrete example from this chapter: Lookup reads file names with a wildcard, ForEach iterates those names, and inside you run a Copy activity that sets the source file name to item(). name and writes to a staging table while adding an additional column with the file name. Note a common pitfall: if Lookup returns an empty array and you do not guard for it, ForEach might run zero iterations and downstream logic expecting completed loads may not run. Use an If Condition to check length or route an On Completion stored procedure that runs only when items exist. Also consider batch count and parallelism: batch count 1 gives sequential behavior; increasing it can speed work but requires idempotent downstream operations. How will you handle ordering requirements when using parallel ForEach?

keyIdea.title: ForEach claim
keyIdea.text: ForEach executes a subgraph for each element in an array; guard it against empty outputs and choose parallelism consciously.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › ForEach Activity
Process

Lookup → ForEach → Copy pattern

Use Lookup to create an array, point ForEach items to that array, and build the copy/transform steps inside the loop.

Example dynamic expression
@activity('GetSalesFiles').output.value
This expression returns the array Lookup produced and is assigned to the ForEach items property. Inside the loop, use @item().name to access the file name.
Batch count and parallelism
Batch count 1 runs sequentially. Increase parallelism to speed copies but ensure downstream stored procedures can handle concurrent writes or use staging that supports parallel ingestion.
Concrete scenario
You have sales_20231026.csv and sales_20231027.csv in a container. Lookup finds both files; ForEach runs one Copy activity per file that maps columns and adds FileName as an additional column so you can trace rows back to their source file in the staging table.
Common mistake
Not checking for empty Lookup output; ForEach will simply skip and a later stored procedure may run with no rows. Add a guard or an If Condition to handle the empty case.
Key Takeaway
ForEach makes repetitive processing simple, but you must handle empties and choose parallelism to match downstream constraints.

screens.title: Lookup Activity and Its Output
screens.narratorSegment: Lookup pulls data from a dataset or query and returns it as JSON that later activities can use. It can return a single first row or an array of rows depending on configuration; when you uncheck 'First row only' you get an array ideal for ForEach. For example, a Lookup against a container directory with a wildcard can return list entries that include a name property for each file. The pipeline then uses that list to drive per-file processing. A useful practice is to inspect and preview Lookup output in ADF Studio to confirm the expected structure before wiring a ForEach to item(). name. A frequent misconception is assuming Lookup will always return rows; if the dataset path or wildcard is wrong the output will be empty, and downstream loops will not run. Handle this by adding an If Condition that checks the array length or by tracking missing files with an On Completion step. Finally, be mindful of permissions: the linked service used by Lookup must have read access to the source so results are accurate. How might you test Lookup output in your environment before running a production pipeline?

keyIdea.title: Lookup role
keyIdea.text: Lookup produces structured output that commonly feeds ForEach; always validate its returned schema and handle empty results.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Lookup Activity

What Lookup returns

Lookup can return a single row or an array. When it returns an array, ForEach can iterate its entries. Preview the output to confirm the property names you will reference.

Sample Lookup output (simplified)
[
  { "name": "sales_20231026.csv" },
  { "name": "sales_20231027.csv" }
]
This array gives ForEach two items; inside the loop use an expression to read the current file name and pass it to Copy.
Practical checks
  • Preview Lookup in Studio to confirm fields like name or FileName exist.
  • Validate linked service permissions to avoid empty results.
  • Guard against empty arrays with an If Condition or an error path.
Common mistake
Assuming Lookup returns a non-empty array; always validate or add fallbacks.

screens.title: If Condition vs Switch
screens.narratorSegment: If Condition and Switch both route execution but solve different needs. Use If Condition when you have a boolean check: true leads to one set of activities and false to another. A typical example is a data validation flag: if validation passes, continue to load; if it fails, send an alert. Switch is best when one input can take many values and each value maps to a different branch — for example, a DataSourceType parameter that can be S Q L, Blob, or A P I. Switch selects one matching case to execute. A common misconception is using nested If Conditions to simulate a multi-case switch; this becomes hard to manage when cases grow. Another practical point: Switch simplifies clear single-value routing and is easier to maintain when each case is distinct. Also consider the default or fallback branch for both constructs to catch unexpected values. Closing question: if you had three source types and shared preprocessing steps, would you use Switch with common pre-step outside it or duplicate those steps inside each case? Think about duplication vs readability. If Condition vs Switch means if for boolean decisions, switch for multiple discrete cases; prefer switch when many distinct paths exist.. In practical terms, when to use boolean branching versus multi-case routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: If for boolean decisions, Switch for multiple discrete cases; prefer Switch when many distinct paths exist.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › If vs Switch
If Condition

Boolean branching

Use when you evaluate a true/false expression. Ideal for validation checks and simple gating.

Simple
Example: if validationResult is true then run Stored Procedure else send notification via Web Activity.
Switch

Multi-case routing

Use when an expression can take multiple named values and each value requires a different path.

Multi-case
Example: DataSourceType equals 'SQL', 'Blob', or 'API' and each case runs a tailored ingest branch.
Design tip
Avoid nesting many If Conditions; prefer Switch for clarity. Put shared preprocessing outside the Switch to avoid duplication unless each case requires unique steps.

screens.title: Transformation Activities
screens.narratorSegment: Transformation activities call external compute to perform logic that is better executed outside a simple copy. Stored Procedure Activity runs database logic where relational engines are efficient—good for cleansing, aggregation, and moving rows between staging and production. Databricks Notebook Activity runs Spark-based notebooks and is ideal for large-scale transformations, flattening nested JSON, and machine learning pre-processing. Azure Function Activity invokes small pieces of custom code for lightweight tasks like sending notifications or small lookups. A practical example in this chapter shows copying raw CSV into a staging table then calling a stored procedure usp_ProcessSalesData to validate and merge rows. A common error is invoking heavy transformations in Functions when a Databricks notebook is more suitable; choose the execution environment by scale and cost. Also ensure the ADF managed identity or linked service has permission to execute stored procedures or run notebooks. Key takeaway: match the transformation activity to the compute profile of the work and keep orchestration separate from heavy compute. Transformation Activities means select stored procedures for relational work, databricks for large-scale spark transforms, and functions for small custom tasks.. In practical terms, stored procedure, databricks notebook, and azure function — choose the right tool. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Transformation Activities
Stored Procedure
Run existing relational logic in Azure SQL or Synapse. Good for set-based cleansing and merges.
Databricks Notebook
Run Spark notebooks for big data transforms, schema flattening, or machine learning preparation.
Azure Function
Invoke small custom code for notifications, lookups, or lightweight API interactions.
Example: sales pipeline
Copy raw CSV to staging, then call a stored procedure named usp_ProcessSalesData passing the target table name to perform validation and merge into production tables.

screens.title: Stored Procedure Activity and Pipeline Example
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows the practical steps to persist data and trigger relational processing. First create a staging table to hold raw CSV rows with a FileName column so you can trace origins. The chapter provides a create table statement for DailySalesStaging; running it prepares your sink for copies. Next, build a pipeline where Lookup returns file names and ForEach copies each file into DailySalesStaging, adding FileName as an additional column. After the ForEach completes, add a Stored Procedure activity to call usp_ProcessSalesData and pass TableToLoad as a parameter so the database-side logic handles validation and merging. A concrete pitfall to avoid: ensure the ADF managed identity or the linked service has permission to execute the stored procedure and to write to the staging table. Also consider whether to truncate the staging table before copies; the chapter suggests a pre-copy script but notes append vs truncate has implications for concurrency and auditing. Final thought: always test the pipeline with a small set of files and confirm the stored procedure runs as expected in Monitor before scaling up. In practical terms, create staging, copy files, then invoke a stored procedure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Practical pipeline
keyIdea.text: Combine Lookup, ForEach, Copy, and Stored Procedure to process multiple files and apply relational transformations after ingestion.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Stored Procedure Walkthrough
Create staging table (example)
CREATE TABLE [dbo].[DailySalesStaging] (
  [ID] INT,
  [Product] NVARCHAR(100),
  [Quantity] INT,
  [FileName] NVARCHAR(255) -- To track source file
);
After the table exists, configure a sink dataset pointing to this table and use Copy activity's Additional columns feature to add FileName with value item().name.
Stored procedure call (concept)
Configure the Stored Procedure activity to call usp_ProcessSalesData and pass the table name or other parameters so the database executes cleansing and merges. Ensure linked service permissions allow execution.
Pipeline sequence
  1. GetSalesFiles (Lookup) returns file list
  2. IterateSalesFiles (ForEach) uses output value as items
  3. Inside ForEach: CopyCurrentSalesFile writes into DailySalesStaging
  4. After ForEach: Stored Procedure activity runs usp_ProcessSalesData
Key Takeaway
Keep ingestion and transformation responsibilities separated and validate permissions before triggering the pipeline.

screens.title: Databricks Notebook and Azure Function Activities
screens.narratorSegment: Choose Databricks when transformations require distributed computing, heavy parsing, or handling nested and unstructured data at scale. Databricks notebooks run on Spark clusters and are appropriate for flattening JSON, partitioned writes, or ML pre-processing. Use Azure Function activities when you need a small, targeted code execution — for instance to send custom notifications, perform a simple enrichment lookup, or call a third-party A P I. A design pattern is to keep heavy, stateful transformations in Databricks and lightweight, stateless tasks in Functions. Common pitfalls include using Functions for large data transformations — they can time out or become costly — and forgetting to grant ADF or managed identity permissions to submit jobs or invoke functions. Also consider deployment and operational concerns: notebooks can be versioned and scheduled, functions should be idempotent for retries, and both should surface logs for debugging. Ask yourself: does this work need distributed compute or a short-lived A P I? Choose the activity accordingly. screens.title: Error Handling and Retry Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Robust pipelines expect failures and plan responses. Configure retry policies on activities to handle transient issues: set a retry count and an interval so a temporary network blip does not trigger a full pipeline failure. Use dependency types to attach different downstream responses: On Success runs only if the predecessor succeeds, On Failure runs only if it fails and is ideal for notifications or compensating actions, On Completion runs regardless and is useful for cleanup, and On Skipped triggers when an activity was skipped. The Fail activity explicitly stops execution and marks the pipeline as failed with a clear message, commonly used within an On Failure branch. For example, if a stored procedure fails repeatedly, an On Failure path can call a Web Activity to post to a Teams channel, then invoke Fail to stop further work. A common mistake is configuring retries without idempotency — ensure the retried activity won't double-write or corrupt data. Test your error flows with simulated failures so monitors and alerts work as intended. How will you balance retries against time-sensitive SLA requirements? Error Handling and Retry Policies means combine activity retries with explicit on failure and on completion paths to handle transient and permanent errors safely.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Error Handling
Retry Policy
Activity-level
Set retries and retry interval on activities to handle transient faults. Example: retry up to 3 times with a 30-second interval for a stored procedure subject to transient network faults.
Dependency types
  • On Success — runs when predecessor succeeds
  • On Failure — runs when predecessor fails
  • On Completion — runs regardless of outcome
  • On Skipped — runs if predecessor was skipped
Example flow
If StoredProcedure fails after retries, On Failure -> Web Activity posts a notification and then Fail activity marks the pipeline as failed with a clear message for operators.
Common mistake
Retrying non-idempotent operations can duplicate writes. Ensure operations are safe to retry or add compensating logic.

screens.title: Parameters, Variables, and Expressions
screens.narratorSegment: Parameters and variables let you avoid hard-coded values and reuse pipelines in different contexts. Pipeline parameters are inputs provided at trigger time — for example a LoadDate parameter can make the same pipeline load data for any date. Variables are internal to a pipeline and can hold counters or intermediate results during execution. Use expressions to reference these values: for example, an expression that accesses a pipeline parameter might read pipeline(). parameters. LoadDate, while using activity output looks like activity('LookupActivity'). output. firstRow. TableName. Practically, you might pass a TableToLoad parameter into a Stored Procedure activity so the same pipeline can process different tables. Watch out for expression syntax mistakes: incorrect casing or wrong property names will cause evaluation errors. A good test is to preview dynamic content and run a pipeline with sample parameters. Finally, combine variables and ForEach to maintain counters or build composite strings — but remember variables are mutable only within a pipeline execution. Closing question: which values in your pipelines are stable deployment settings and which should be parameters at runtime? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to move beyond simple copies and design pipelines that think and adapt. Control flow activities give your pipeline decision-making power — they let you iterate over items, branch on conditions, and route work to different processing paths. Transformation activities let ADF call external compute, like stored procedures, Databricks notebooks, or Azure Functions, so heavy processing happens where it belongs. We'll show common patterns — lookup a set of files, iterate with ForEach, and run copies and transforms — and then cover retry policies and success or failure paths so the whole pipeline stays resilient. You will also see how parameters and variables make pipelines reusable across days, tables, and environments, and how expressions link activity output into later steps. A concrete use case we return to is processing daily sales files: use Lookup to get file names, ForEach to copy each file, then run a stored procedure to merge results. By the end you will recognize when to use control flow vs transformation activities and how to guard a pipeline with retries and failure handlers. Consider how your own ETL jobs could be made dynamic and more reliable.

These objectives focus on practical pipeline design and reusable logic. First, you will learn to use control flow activities — ForEach, If Condition, and Switch — so pipelines can iterate and branch. That means you can process many files or route work to the correct ingestion path. Second, you'll integrate transformation activities such as Stored Procedure, Databricks Notebook, and Lookup to perform data processing where it is most efficient, whether inside a database or on a Spark cluster. Each objective includes why that skill matters: iteration reduces manual work, transformations centralize heavy compute, and branching keeps flows maintainable. You will also practice implementing error handling patterns and retry policies so transient failures don't cause service disruptions. Finally, you'll use parameters and variables to make pipelines flexible across schedules and environments, which reduces duplication and deployment friction. Each of these skills maps to a verified competency milestone so you can measure your progress and apply these patterns to real ingestion jobs.

Beyond concept familiarity, these objectives prepare you for hands-on pipeline construction. You will be able to author a Lookup that returns multiple items and feed that output into a ForEach loop to process each element. You will also compose an execution sequence in which copies and transformations run in order, and you will attach On Failure handlers to notify and stop processing when appropriate. The lab uses real artifacts: create a generic DelimitedText dataset for raw CSV files and a staging S Q L table, then build a pipeline called DynamicSalesIngestionPipeline that demonstrates Lookup, ForEach, Copy, and a Stored Procedure call. Practice configuring an activity retry policy for transient errors and check the Monitor tab to confirm runs and retries. These tasks map closely to the assessment idea in the chapter, so completing them will show you can implement a typical production ingestion with error handling and parameterized inputs.

Control flow activities define how and when work runs inside a pipeline. At a simple level, they are the glue that orders activities, evaluates conditions, and iterates over collections. Think of control flow as the program structure for pipeline orchestration: ForEach repeats a set of activities for each item in an array, If Condition chooses between two branches based on a boolean expression, and Switch selects among many branches based on a value. Lookup is often the source of truth for collections — it returns arrays that drive ForEach. These activities matter because real data integration rarely processes exactly one file or table; you often need to loop, branch, and make decisions based on metadata or runtime results. A common misconception is treating control flow like transformation: control flow does not change data; instead it controls which processing steps run. For example, you might use Lookup to fetch today's file list, then ForEach to copy each file, then a Switch to handle different source formats. Key takeaway: separate orchestration (control flow) from transformation so pipelines stay flexible and easier to debug. How would you test a branch that handles a rare source type?

ForEach is how you process many similar items with the same set of activities. The expected pattern is: first use a Lookup activity to return an array of items, then set the ForEach items property to that output so each entry becomes an iteration context. Inside the ForEach you can run Copy, Stored Procedure, Databricks, or any activity; each iteration sees its own current item accessible via item() expressions. A concrete example from this chapter: Lookup reads file names with a wildcard, ForEach iterates those names, and inside you run a Copy activity that sets the source file name to item(). name and writes to a staging table while adding an additional column with the file name. Note a common pitfall: if Lookup returns an empty array and you do not guard for it, ForEach might run zero iterations and downstream logic expecting completed loads may not run. Use an If Condition to check length or route an On Completion stored procedure that runs only when items exist. Also consider batch count and parallelism: batch count 1 gives sequential behavior; increasing it can speed work but requires idempotent downstream operations. How will you handle ordering requirements when using parallel ForEach?

Lookup pulls data from a dataset or query and returns it as JSON that later activities can use. It can return a single first row or an array of rows depending on configuration; when you uncheck 'First row only' you get an array ideal for ForEach. For example, a Lookup against a container directory with a wildcard can return list entries that include a name property for each file. The pipeline then uses that list to drive per-file processing. A useful practice is to inspect and preview Lookup output in ADF Studio to confirm the expected structure before wiring a ForEach to item(). name. A frequent misconception is assuming Lookup will always return rows; if the dataset path or wildcard is wrong the output will be empty, and downstream loops will not run. Handle this by adding an If Condition that checks the array length or by tracking missing files with an On Completion step. Finally, be mindful of permissions: the linked service used by Lookup must have read access to the source so results are accurate. How might you test Lookup output in your environment before running a production pipeline?

If Condition and Switch both route execution but solve different needs. Use If Condition when you have a boolean check: true leads to one set of activities and false to another. A typical example is a data validation flag: if validation passes, continue to load; if it fails, send an alert. Switch is best when one input can take many values and each value maps to a different branch — for example, a DataSourceType parameter that can be S Q L, Blob, or A P I. Switch selects one matching case to execute. A common misconception is using nested If Conditions to simulate a multi-case switch; this becomes hard to manage when cases grow. Another practical point: Switch simplifies clear single-value routing and is easier to maintain when each case is distinct. Also consider the default or fallback branch for both constructs to catch unexpected values. Closing question: if you had three source types and shared preprocessing steps, would you use Switch with common pre-step outside it or duplicate those steps inside each case? Think about duplication vs readability. If Condition vs Switch means if for boolean decisions, switch for multiple discrete cases; prefer switch when many distinct paths exist.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transformation activities call external compute to perform logic that is better executed outside a simple copy. Stored Procedure Activity runs database logic where relational engines are efficient—good for cleansing, aggregation, and moving rows between staging and production. Databricks Notebook Activity runs Spark-based notebooks and is ideal for large-scale transformations, flattening nested JSON, and machine learning pre-processing. Also ensure the ADF managed identity or linked service has permission to execute stored procedures or run notebooks.
